title: Better Observation for Better Feedback
author: Rod J. Naquin
summary: Rod Naquin, mentoring a student teacher, describes how he abandoned an unwieldy observation checklist for two simple back-of-the-room routines: a seating-chart tally that codes each teacher response to a student as evaluation, correction or push, and a five-minute count of off-task students. He then draws on research to argue that the type of feedback matters more than the amount, citing a 435-study analysis in which task-focused feedback far outperformed praise or rewards. He connects this to Nystrand's classroom-talk studies, where the default initiate-respond-evaluate pattern shuts down open discussion unless teachers take up what students actually say. The same rules, he argues, govern how leaders respond to teachers in post-observation debriefs, where most feedback is a stack of evaluations with one correction. He also flags the limits of observation, noting that even Nuthall's team missed about 40 percent of the talk its microphones caught. The piece ends with a practical talk move for debriefs: repeat a phrase the teacher used, then ask a question built on it.
points: Tallying each teacher response as evaluation, correction or push on a seating chart turns vague advice to give more feedback into a concrete pattern a coach can point to.
The type of feedback matters more than the quantity: feedback on the task and how to approach it had roughly four times the effect of reward-style feedback, and some feedback is actively harmful.

Post-observation conferences usually run on the same initiate-respond-evaluate script that stifles classroom discussion, so leaders should practice uptake on teachers' own words instead of delivering verdicts.

Counting off-task students every five minutes with a fixed definition gives a pattern to question, but observers see only a slice of any lesson and should open debriefs with questions rather than scores.
quotes: Thirty marks tells you a teacher is busy. Thirty E’s tells you what to work on.
If we wouldn’t accept a classroom running on “good job,” we shouldn’t run our coaching on it either.
A coach asks, “What could you have done differently?” and already has the answer in mind. The teacher guesses. The coach evaluates. That’s recitation with grown-ups.
A quiet team meeting can mean agreement, or it can mean people have checked out, and from the head of the table those look the same.
Nuthall’s team, with an observer assigned to every student, still missed about 40 percent of the talk their microphones caught. A leader who watched 20 minutes of a lesson saw a slice of it.
Repeat a phrase they actually used, then ask a question built on it. “You said they checked out around minute 20. What were they doing right before that?
If your advice is good, it will still be good after one more question. If it’s off, the question just saved you from giving it.
